uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a1.text: Almost every bacterium is a single cell.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a2.text: Most are about a micrometre across. Far too small to see.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a3.text: And yet, under a microscope, they come in more shapes than you'd think.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a4.text: Long before DNA tests, the microscope was all there was. And even today, a lab's first clue is the shape of the cells.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a5.text: Round cells are cocci. From the Greek kokkos: a grain, or a berry.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a6.text: Rod-shaped cells are bacilli. Latin for a little rod.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a7.text: And then there are the spirals.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a8.text: But a bacterium rarely stays alone for long.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b1.text: Bacteria multiply by splitting in two. And sometimes, the two halves don't let go.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b2.text: Split once and stay joined, and you get a pair. A diplococcus. Diplo means double.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b3.text: Keep splitting in the same direction, and the pairs become chains: streptococci.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b4.text: Streptos is Greek for pliant, or twisted. Like a chain.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b5.text: Streptococcus pyogenes is one of these. It gives you strep throat. And, rarely, the flesh-eating infection.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b6.text: Split in two directions, and you get a square of four. A tetrad.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b7.text: Three directions, and you get a little package, up to a cube of eight. A sarcina.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b8.text: And split in a new direction each time... and you get a bunch of grapes.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b9.text: Staphylococcus. Staphyle is Greek for a bunch of grapes.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b10.text: Which makes Staphylococcus aureus the golden grape-bunch berry.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b12.text: It's a common cause of skin infections. And it lives quietly up the nose of about one person in four.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b14.text: So the name often tells you the shape. Cocco, the berry. Strepto, the chain. Staphylo, the grapes.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c1.text: Rods form groups too. In chains, they're streptobacilli.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c2.text: Corynebacterium snaps when it divides, instead of splitting cleanly. So its rods end up side by side, like a fence... or at angles, in Vs and Ys.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c3.text: Some rods have quite a career.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c4.text: Clostridium botulinum makes botulinum toxin. The most lethal biological toxin known.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c5.text: In tiny, purified doses, it's also Botox. People pay to have it injected into their faces.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c6.text: Between the round and the rod sits the coccobacillus: a rod so short, it's almost round.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c7.text: Haemophilus influenzae is one. It was first described in the 1890s, by a scientist who thought it caused the flu.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c8.text: It doesn't. Flu is caused by a virus. The name stuck anyway.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c9.text: Yersinia pestis is another one. Small, plump, and the cause of the Black Death.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c10.text: In the mid-1300s, it killed at least a third of Europe.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d2.text: A vibrio is a curved rod. A comma.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d3.text: Its name comes from the Latin for vibrate, because it looks like it's vibrating as it swims.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d4.text: Vibrio cholerae causes cholera. This little comma has ended a great many sentences.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d5.text: Even now, it's thought to kill tens of thousands of people a year.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d6.text: A spirillum is a thick, stiff spiral, with tufts of flagella at each end.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d7.text: And a spirochete is a thin, flexible corkscrew, with a trick: its flagella are inside the cell.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d8.text: In open water, spirochetes are slowpokes. In thick, gel-like places, they do better than you'd expect.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d9.text: Treponema pallidum, which causes syphilis, is one. So is Borrelia, which ticks carry, and which causes Lyme disease.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e1.text: And then there are the odd ones.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e2.text: Streptomyces grows as branching threads, like a tiny fungus.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e3.text: It makes geosmin: the earthy smell of soil after rain. And more than two-thirds of the useful antibiotics that come from nature.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e4.text: Some bacteria are shaped like flat, six-pointed stars.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e5.text: Caulobacter grows a stalk, with glue on the end. One of the strongest natural glues known.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e6.text: When it divides, one daughter swims away. The other stays stuck.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e7.text: Mycoplasma has no cell wall at all. So it has no fixed shape.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e9.text: Thiomargarita magnifica, described in 2022, grows to about a centimetre long. A single bacterium you can see with your own eyes.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e10.text: One last shape is a trap.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e11.text: Haloquadratum is a flat, square cell from very salty water. And it is not a bacterium at all. It's an archaeon.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f1.text: So why have a shape at all?

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f2.text: First, something has to hold it. That's the cell wall: a tough mesh around the cell.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f3.text: Take the wall away, and the cell goes round, or shapeless. Just like Mycoplasma.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f4.text: Second, food. A bacterium feeds through its surface, and small cells have a lot of surface for their size. That's one big reason bacteria stay small.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f5.text: Growing into long threads adds even more surface to feed through.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f6.text: Third, getting around. Helicobacter pylori lives in the mucus of the stomach. Its spiral cells swim a little faster there than straight ones.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f7.text: And scientists think shape also helps bacteria stick to things, and avoid being eaten.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:w1.text: Spheres, rods, commas, corkscrews, stars, and giants. Every one of them, a single cell.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:w2.text: And the shape is only the first clue. Next time: the purple and pink stain that splits bacteria into two great teams.
